# HI5T0RY: Dawn Staley, First USA Basketball Olympic Flag Bearer
**Author**Brooklee Han
**share**Share on TwitterShare on FacebookShare on Email
February 6, 2024
_As part of its 50th Anniversary, USA Basketball is celebrating 50 iconic moments from the organization's history._
Despite a robust collection of Olympic medals, the vast majority being gold, a USA Basketball athlete was not nominated to serve as Olympic Opening Ceremony flag bearer until 2004, exactly 100 years after the spot was first exhibited in an Olympic Games.
The woman tasked with the honor was legendary USA Basketball athlete, and now coach, **Dawn Staley**.
The 2004 Summer Games in Athens, marked Staley’s third trip to the Olympics. A point guard, Staley had helped USA Basketball claim gold in 1996 in Atlanta and 2000 in Sydney. Her Olympic winning streak would continue in Athens, as Staley and the USA beat out Australia 74-63 to clinch gold in the women’s final.

Born and raised in Philadelphia, Staley is the youngest of five children. Staley’s talent on the court was evident from a young age, as she was named the national high school player of the year during her final high school season. She went on to play for four seasons at the University of Virginia before traveling to Europe to play professionally for two seasons. In 1996 she made her U.S. professional basketball debut when she was drafted to play for the American Basketball League’s Richmond Rage. Staley played with the Richmond Rage until 1999, when she moved over to the WNBA, playing for the Charlotte Sting. She remained at part of the Charlotte Sting for eight seasons before retiring from the sport.

# HI5T0RY: Dawn Staley, First USA Basketball Olympic Flag Bearer
During her time in the WNBA Staley began coaching at Temple University during her off seasons, before being hired by the University of South Carolina in 2008 as the head coach of the Gamecocks. Under Staley’s guidance, the South Carolina Gamecocks have captured five SEC regular season championships and two NCAA titles.

Staley’s career as a USA Basketball coach began in 2006, when she we brought in as an assistant coach for the World Championship team. She would go on to serve as an assistant coach for the 2008 and 2016 U.S. Olympic teams. In 2017, Staley was named the head coach of the USA Basketball’s Women’s team through the 2020 Olympics. In Tokyo, Staley became the first Black woman to coach an Olympic team to gold, while her athlete and former teammate Sue Bird became just the second USA Basketball athlete to serve as flag bearer.
Following her USA Basketball coaching career, Staley continues to serve as a member of the USA Women’s National Team Committee.

# A Look Back: Dawn Staley Carrying The U.S. Flag At The 2004 Olympics - WNBA
## A Look Back: Dawn Staley Carrying The U.S. Flag At The 2004 Olympics
Thu, Aug 12, 2004, 3:26 PM
/
WNBA.com
**NEW YORK, August 12, 2004 –** The United States Olympic Committee announced today that Charlotte Sting point guard and two-time Olympic gold medalist Dawn Staley will serve as the flag bearer for the entire United States Olympic contingent during the Opening Ceremonies of the Athens Olympic Games. NBC will televise the Opening Ceremonies beginning at 8 p.m. ET on August 13.
“I am in disbelief.” Staley told NBC’s Katie Couric this morning on the set of the Today Show in Athens. “I am a little girl from North Philadelphia in the housing projects . . . leading our U.S. delegation into the Opening Ceremony. It’s a tremendous honor. I am still in total disbelief.”
Staley was chosen by a vote of the captains of all the U.S. teams.
“I’m not an emotional person, but this makes me emotional,” Staley added. “I’m invisible most of the time. I’m not even a conversation starter. I usually do all my talking on the court, so it’s an honor that so many other sports see me in a different light.”
Staley, who won Olympic Gold in 1996 in Atlanta and in 2000 in Sydney, is a six-year veteran of the WNBA, and led the Charlotte Sting to the WNBA Finals in 2001. She is a three-time WNBA All-Star, and is the career leader in assists for women’s professional basketball players (1,601 in two ABL seasons and five-plus WNBA seasons). During the WNBA offseason, Staley serves as the head women’s basketball coach at Temple University, leading the Owls to a pair of NCAA Tournament berths over the past four years.
Staley has also been honored on numerous occasions for her work with inner-city Philadelphia children through the foundation that bears her name, winning the 1999 WNBA Entrepreneurial Spirit Award, and the 1998 American Red Cross Spectrum Award, which celebrates women who have made outstanding contributions to their communities.

# HI5T0RY: Dawn Staley, First USA Basketball Olympic Flag Bearer
**Author**Brooklee Han
**share**Share on TwitterShare on FacebookShare on Email
February 6, 2024
_As part of its 50th Anniversary, USA Basketball is celebrating 50 iconic moments from the organization's history._
Despite a robust collection of Olympic medals, the vast majority being gold, a USA Basketball athlete was not nominated to serve as Olympic Opening Ceremony flag bearer until 2004, exactly 100 years after the spot was first exhibited in an Olympic Games.
The woman tasked with the honor was legendary USA Basketball athlete, and now coach, **Dawn Staley**.
The 2004 Summer Games in Athens, marked Staley’s third trip to the Olympics. A point guard, Staley had helped USA Basketball claim gold in 1996 in Atlanta and 2000 in Sydney. Her Olympic winning streak would continue in Athens, as Staley and the USA beat out Australia 74-63 to clinch gold in the women’s final.

Born and raised in Philadelphia, Staley is the youngest of five children. Staley’s career as a USA Basketball coach began in 2006, when she we brought in as an assistant coach for the World Championship team. She would go on to serve as an assistant coach for the 2008 and 2016 U.S. Olympic teams. In 2017, Staley was named the head coach of the USA Basketball’s Women’s team through the 2020 Olympics. In Tokyo, Staley became the first Black woman to coach an Olympic team to gold, while her athlete and former teammate Sue Bird became just the second USA Basketball athlete to serve as flag bearer.
Following her USA Basketball coaching career, Staley continues to serve as a member of the USA Women’s National Team Committee.

# A Look Back: Dawn Staley Carrying The U.S. Flag At The 2004 Olympics - WNBA
## A Look Back: Dawn Staley Carrying The U.S. Flag At The 2004 Olympics
Thu, Aug 12, 2004, 3:26 PM
/
WNBA.com
**NEW YORK, August 12, 2004 –** The United States Olympic Committee announced today that Charlotte Sting point guard and two-time Olympic gold medalist Dawn Staley will serve as the flag bearer for the entire United States Olympic contingent during the Opening Ceremonies of the Athens Olympic Games. NBC will televise the Opening Ceremonies beginning at 8 p.m. ET on August 13.
“I am in disbelief.” Staley told NBC’s Katie Couric this morning on the set of the Today Show in Athens. “I am a little girl from North Philadelphia in the housing projects . . . leading our U.S. delegation into the Opening Ceremony. It’s a tremendous honor. I am still in total disbelief.”
Staley was chosen by a vote of the captains of all the U.S. teams.
“I’m not an emotional person, but this makes me emotional,” Staley added. “I’m invisible most of the time. I’m not even a conversation starter. I usually do all my talking on the court, so it’s an honor that so many other sports see me in a different light.”
Staley, who won Olympic Gold in 1996 in Atlanta and in 2000 in Sydney, is a six-year veteran of the WNBA, and led the Charlotte Sting to the WNBA Finals in 2001. She is a three-time WNBA All-Star, and is the career leader in assists for women’s professional basketball players (1,601 in two ABL seasons and five-plus WNBA seasons). During the WNBA offseason, Staley serves as the head women’s basketball coach at Temple University, leading the Owls to a pair of NCAA Tournament berths over the past four years.
Staley has also been honored on numerous occasions for her work with inner-city Philadelphia children through the foundation that bears her name, winning the 1999 WNBA Entrepreneurial Spirit Award, and the 1998 American Red Cross Spectrum Award, which celebrates women who have made outstanding contributions to their communities.

The **opening ceremony** of the **2004 Summer Olympics** was held on August 13, 2004 starting at 20:45 EEST (UTC+3) at the Olympic Stadium in Marousi, Greece, a suburb of Athens.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-ingr2-2) As mandated by the Olympic Charter, the proceedings combined the formal and ceremonial opening of this international sporting event, including welcoming speeches, hoisting of the flags and the parade of athletes, with an artistic spectacle to showcase the host nation's culture and history. 72,000 spectators (with nearly 50 world leaders) attended the event, with approximately 15,000 athletes from 202 countries participating in the ceremony as well. It marked the first-ever international broadcast of high-definition television, undertaken by the U.S. media conglomerate NBC Universal and the Japanese broadcaster NHK. The Games were officially opened by President of the Hellenic RepublicKonstantinos Stephanopoulos at 23:46 EEST (UTC+3).
Fireworks

### Countdown and Welcome
[edit]
The opening ceremony began with a 28-second countdown—one second per Olympics held since Athens last hosted the first modern games, paced by the sounds of an amplified heartbeat. At the end of the countdown, fireworks were set off.
Four hundred percussionists performed the zeimbekiko before marching around the edge of the flooded stadium grounds, accompanied by a 50-person strong bouzouki band. The performance was led by two drummers, one inside the stadium and one projected on the stadium screen from the ancient stadium of Olympia, the locale of the Olympic games in antiquity. On screen was Petros Kourtis,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-bovary-4) with Nikos Hatzidavitidis[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-5) responding live at the ceremony. A blazing comet, seemingly coming from the ancient stadium of Olympia, lands on the flooded stadium floor drawing the Olympic Rings with its fire. The comet symbolizes the fire of the ancients giving life to the modern Olympic movement, thus bridging the past and the present together. According to Dimitris Papaioannou, the event "was a pageant of traditional Greek culture and history harkening back to its mythological beginnings, and viewed through the progression of Greek art."
Next, a young Greek boy, Michalis Patsatzis, sailed into the stadium on a giant paper boat waving the host nation's flag, symbolizing Greece's maritime tradition and its close connection to the sea. The Hellenic Naval Band then walks into the stadium. The President of the Athens Organizing Committee for the Olympic Games (ATHOC), Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki, and President of the International Olympic CommitteeJacques Rogge walk onto the stadium floor. The Band then performs the Presidential fanfare, where President of the Hellenic RepublicKonstantinos Stephanopoulos then also arrives on the stadium floor. The three presidents meet the young boy, before Hymn to Liberty, the Greek national anthem was performed a cappella with the raising of the Greek Flag.

### Countdown and Welcome
The segments that followed were divided in two main parts. The first part of the main artistic segment of the opening ceremony was called "Allegory." "Allegory" introduced the main conceptual themes and ideals that are going to be omnipresent throughout the entire opening ceremony, such as the confluence of the past and present, love and passion as the progenitors of history, and humanity's attempt to understand itself. The second part, called the "Clepsydra," or "Hourglass," celebrates the themes introduced in the "Allegory" section through a portrayal of Greek history from the ancient to the modern times.

### Countdown and Welcome
The "Allegory" segment begins with a recitation of a verse from Nobel Prize-winning Greek poet George Seferis' poem "Mythistorema 3." As the verse is being recited on the speakers, the spotlights are focused upon a woman clad in a black gown looking out to the water. Holding a marble sculpture head, the woman seems to be entering into a dream. As she looks into the dark water, a centaur appears whose human and animal parts supposedly symbolize the duality of spirit and body. The centaur then walks about and then throws a spear of light into the center of the stadium, from which a giant statue that exemplifies Cycladic art (and thus one of the first depictions of the human form in Greek art) emerges. This Cycladic head also represents one of the first attempts of humanity to understand itself. With the use of lasers, geometrical shapes and other scientific images (such as a stylistic representation of the Solar System) are displayed on the figure's face. The statue then breaks into pieces that float away, and from within it emerges a smaller kouros statue from the Archaic Period of Greek sculpture, which in turn breaks apart to reveal the depiction of man in a sculpture of the classical period, symbolizing the dawn of individuality and extolling human scale, one of the principal themes of the 2004 Olympics. At the end of this sequence, a cube arises from the water, and a man starts slowly balancing himself on the rotating cube while representations of humankind's greatest achievements, contrasted to humanistic representations and images of people of various ethnicities and ages, are projected onto the pieces of broken sculpture, which seem to be floating above the water. This last sequence is meant to symbolize the birth of logical thought, higher learning, and humanity finally making sense of the world in which it lives. After this sequence, the pieces of sculpture descend to the water, meant to symbolize the Greek isles.

by Bob Fisher 14 Aug 2004 09:28 BST
The symbolism of Greek history, inevitably intertwined with mythology, formed the basis of the introduction of the athletes at the Olympic Stadium, linking, as it did, the emergence of the country and its peoples from the elements. It had the surreal overtones of water ballet and moving Elgin marbles and was held close to the floodlit monuments of the Acropolis to display the spirit of Athens. It was played to a packed stadium where every IOC member and other VIPs came under the spotlight at some time.
The parade of athletes was led by a Greek flag – the tradition is that Greece, as the founder of the Games, is a permanent host – but not the team as the host nation’s athletes, as is good manners, leave the stadium open to the guests and bring up the rear. The Greek alphabet produced a new order, one that seemed even to those who understood, a touch bizarre when St’ Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines, and San Marino all came in ahead of Angola. It baffled even more when the USA came in immediately after Zimbabwe and just before Japan; Great Britain slotted between Mauretania and Mexico!
It became obvious that the bigger nations were not producing all of their athletes and only four of Britain’s sailors were amongst Team GB – the Star crew, Iain Percy and Steve Mitchell, and the Tornado pairing of Leigh McMillan and Mark Bulkeley – as they “marched” into the stadium. Most of the rest were sailing the following day and the ceremony went on past midnight and the transport system back home is insufferably slow.
Marching is a thing of the past; there is much greater informality about the entry of the athletes – it is a happy occasion and it had its highlights. Among them was the appearance of the flag carrier for Madagascar – quite the pick of the show – and the cheer that greeted the small contingent from Iraq. Interestingly, Denmark was remarked on being the country of Paul Elvstrom and Canada was cheered in by the ISAF President’s daughter, Martha, waving a huge Canadian flag. Maybe it was simply politically correct that the Afghanistan team was led by a woman, bearing in mind how the rest of her gender are treated in that country.

The Blairs, Tony and Cherie, cheered the British team’s entry enthusiastically. It was led by flag bearer, Kate Howie, the most senior member of the British judo team. Representation that Iain Percy, a Sydney gold medallist, should carry the flag had been made, but he lost the vote to Howie.
The athletes, after completing a circuit of the track were assembled in the centre of the arena – the ingredients of what appeared to resemble a giant confection on completion - with the Greek contingent in their beige jackets providing the final icing on the cake. And then there were fireworks (almost certainly coincidental with those at Cowes to mark the end of the Week), spectacular, as might be expected, to mark the homecoming of the Olympic Games.
After a rather odd contribution from Bjork, there was a reminder of all the cities of the Modern Olympics with two gaps for the interruptions of the World Wars, before the Presidents of ATHOC, Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki, and the IOC, Jacques Rogge, began their long walk to the podium, where under an Olive tree (the olive branch symbolism was everywhere) they welcomed everyone to Athens and gave the Olympic Games a Welcome Home. Rogge began his speech, to tumultuous applause, in Greek before using the other two official languages of the Olympic, French and English.
Jacques Rogge, the IOC President, has a long connection with sailing, dating back to his win of the Cadet Championship at Burnham-on-Crouch and on through two Olympics in the Finn class, where today his son, Philippe, is the class President. He thanked the Greeks, their authorities, and especially the volunteers, before condemning the use of Drugs in sport. As a former Chairman of the IOC Doping Commission, Rogge has a special reason to attack this menace. From his place in the stands, the Greek President, Costis Stefanopoulos, proclaimed a general welcome.
The Olympic flag entered the stadium, borne at shoulder level by eight white suited bearers and completed a spotlighted circuit of the track in the darkened stadium before being handed to members of the Greek Navy for the ceremonial hoisting at the flag pole to match the Greek flag on the other. The 108 years old graphics on the Olympic flag, symbolising the uniting of five continents at the Games, was not lost on many. There were more fireworks when it was fully hoisted.

The Olympic oath was taken and the massive screen in the studio showed a representation of flame turning into a dove and then into a Mercator representation of the world before the Olympic flame was borne into the studio, the end of its round the world journey. There were five runner changes before it was handed to the athlete who climbed the long staircase to light the beacon, that for all the world looks like the blow off of an oil rig, and stand as the beacon was elevated to its position over the stadium.
That athlete was Nikolaos Kaklamanakis, the board sailor who won a gold medal for Greece at Savannah in 1996 and was hailed as the latest in a line of “Greek Gods.” It should be remembered that when King Constantine won gold in the Dragons at Naples in 1960, he was similarly hailed, but that was before the Colonels deposed him. “Niko” is still a darling of the people and featured in poster ads for the Games for more than a year. Lighting the torch was his latest accolade.
The ceremonials over, the Games of the 28th Olympiad can begin.
Full results with mark by mark roundings are at sailing.org/olympics2004

by Bob Fisher 14 Aug 2004 09:28 BST
The symbolism of Greek history, inevitably intertwined with mythology, formed the basis of the introduction of the athletes at the Olympic Stadium, linking, as it did, the emergence of the country and its peoples from the elements. It had the surreal overtones of water ballet and moving Elgin marbles and was held close to the floodlit monuments of the Acropolis to display the spirit of Athens. It was played to a packed stadium where every IOC member and other VIPs came under the spotlight at some time.
The parade of athletes was led by a Greek flag – the tradition is that Greece, as the founder of the Games, is a permanent host – but not the team as the host nation’s athletes, as is good manners, leave the stadium open to the guests and bring up the rear. The Greek alphabet produced a new order, one that seemed even to those who understood, a touch bizarre when St’ Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines, and San Marino all came in ahead of Angola. It baffled even more when the USA came in immediately after Zimbabwe and just before Japan; Great Britain slotted between Mauretania and Mexico!
It became obvious that the bigger nations were not producing all of their athletes and only four of Britain’s sailors were amongst Team GB – the Star crew, Iain Percy and Steve Mitchell, and the Tornado pairing of Leigh McMillan and Mark Bulkeley – as they “marched” into the stadium. Most of the rest were sailing the following day and the ceremony went on past midnight and the transport system back home is insufferably slow.
Marching is a thing of the past; there is much greater informality about the entry of the athletes – it is a happy occasion and it had its highlights. Among them was the appearance of the flag carrier for Madagascar – quite the pick of the show – and the cheer that greeted the small contingent from Iraq. Interestingly, Denmark was remarked on being the country of Paul Elvstrom and Canada was cheered in by the ISAF President’s daughter, Martha, waving a huge Canadian flag. Maybe it was simply politically correct that the Afghanistan team was led by a woman, bearing in mind how the rest of her gender are treated in that country.
texts.1:
The Blairs, Tony and Cherie, cheered the British team’s entry enthusiastically. It was led by flag bearer, Kate Howie, the most senior member of the British judo team. Representation that Iain Percy, a Sydney gold medallist, should carry the flag had been made, but he lost the vote to Howie.
The athletes, after completing a circuit of the track were assembled in the centre of the arena – the ingredients of what appeared to resemble a giant confection on completion - with the Greek contingent in their beige jackets providing the final icing on the cake. And then there were fireworks (almost certainly coincidental with those at Cowes to mark the end of the Week), spectacular, as might be expected, to mark the homecoming of the Olympic Games.
After a rather odd contribution from Bjork, there was a reminder of all the cities of the Modern Olympics with two gaps for the interruptions of the World Wars, before the Presidents of ATHOC, Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki, and the IOC, Jacques Rogge, began their long walk to the podium, where under an Olive tree (the olive branch symbolism was everywhere) they welcomed everyone to Athens and gave the Olympic Games a Welcome Home. Rogge began his speech, to tumultuous applause, in Greek before using the other two official languages of the Olympic, French and English.
Jacques Rogge, the IOC President, has a long connection with sailing, dating back to his win of the Cadet Championship at Burnham-on-Crouch and on through two Olympics in the Finn class, where today his son, Philippe, is the class President. He thanked the Greeks, their authorities, and especially the volunteers, before condemning the use of Drugs in sport. As a former Chairman of the IOC Doping Commission, Rogge has a special reason to attack this menace. From his place in the stands, the Greek President, Costis Stefanopoulos, proclaimed a general welcome.
The Olympic flag entered the stadium, borne at shoulder level by eight white suited bearers and completed a spotlighted circuit of the track in the darkened stadium before being handed to members of the Greek Navy for the ceremonial hoisting at the flag pole to match the Greek flag on the other. The 108 years old graphics on the Olympic flag, symbolising the uniting of five continents at the Games, was not lost on many. There were more fireworks when it was fully hoisted.
texts.2:
The Olympic oath was taken and the massive screen in the studio showed a representation of flame turning into a dove and then into a Mercator representation of the world before the Olympic flame was borne into the studio, the end of its round the world journey. There were five runner changes before it was handed to the athlete who climbed the long staircase to light the beacon, that for all the world looks like the blow off of an oil rig, and stand as the beacon was elevated to its position over the stadium.
That athlete was Nikolaos Kaklamanakis, the board sailor who won a gold medal for Greece at Savannah in 1996 and was hailed as the latest in a line of “Greek Gods.” It should be remembered that when King Constantine won gold in the Dragons at Naples in 1960, he was similarly hailed, but that was before the Colonels deposed him. “Niko” is still a darling of the people and featured in poster ads for the Games for more than a year. Lighting the torch was his latest accolade.
The ceremonials over, the Games of the 28th Olympiad can begin.

The **opening ceremony** of the **2004 Summer Olympics** was held on August 13, 2004 starting at 20:45 EEST (UTC+3) at the Olympic Stadium in Marousi, Greece, a suburb of Athens.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-ingr2-2) As mandated by the Olympic Charter, the proceedings combined the formal and ceremonial opening of this international sporting event, including welcoming speeches, hoisting of the flags and the parade of athletes, with an artistic spectacle to showcase the host nation's culture and history. 72,000 spectators (with nearly 50 world leaders) attended the event, with approximately 15,000 athletes from 202 countries participating in the ceremony as well. It marked the first-ever international broadcast of high-definition television, undertaken by the U.S. media conglomerate NBC Universal and the Japanese broadcaster NHK. The Games were officially opened by President of the Hellenic RepublicKonstantinos Stephanopoulos at 23:46 EEST (UTC+3).

### Countdown and Welcome
[edit]
The opening ceremony began with a 28-second countdown—one second per Olympics held since Athens last hosted the first modern games, paced by the sounds of an amplified heartbeat. At the end of the countdown, fireworks were set off.
Four hundred percussionists performed the zeimbekiko before marching around the edge of the flooded stadium grounds, accompanied by a 50-person strong bouzouki band. The performance was led by two drummers, one inside the stadium and one projected on the stadium screen from the ancient stadium of Olympia, the locale of the Olympic games in antiquity. On screen was Petros Kourtis,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-bovary-4) with Nikos Hatzidavitidis[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-5) responding live at the ceremony. A blazing comet, seemingly coming from the ancient stadium of Olympia, lands on the flooded stadium floor drawing the Olympic Rings with its fire. The comet symbolizes the fire of the ancients giving life to the modern Olympic movement, thus bridging the past and the present together. According to Dimitris Papaioannou, the event "was a pageant of traditional Greek culture and history harkening back to its mythological beginnings, and viewed through the progression of Greek art."
Next, a young Greek boy, Michalis Patsatzis, sailed into the stadium on a giant paper boat waving the host nation's flag, symbolizing Greece's maritime tradition and its close connection to the sea. The Hellenic Naval Band then walks into the stadium. The President of the Athens Organizing Committee for the Olympic Games (ATHOC), Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki, and President of the International Olympic CommitteeJacques Rogge walk onto the stadium floor. The Band then performs the Presidential fanfare, where President of the Hellenic RepublicKonstantinos Stephanopoulos then also arrives on the stadium floor. The three presidents meet the young boy, before Hymn to Liberty, the Greek national anthem was performed a cappella with the raising of the Greek Flag.
texts.2:
### Countdown and Welcome
The segments that followed were divided in two main parts. The first part of the main artistic segment of the opening ceremony was called "Allegory." "Allegory" introduced the main conceptual themes and ideals that are going to be omnipresent throughout the entire opening ceremony, such as the confluence of the past and present, love and passion as the progenitors of history, and humanity's attempt to understand itself. The second part, called the "Clepsydra," or "Hourglass," celebrates the themes introduced in the "Allegory" section through a portrayal of Greek history from the ancient to the modern times.
texts.3:
### Countdown and Welcome
The "Allegory" segment begins with a recitation of a verse from Nobel Prize-winning Greek poet George Seferis' poem "Mythistorema 3." As the verse is being recited on the speakers, the spotlights are focused upon a woman clad in a black gown looking out to the water. Holding a marble sculpture head, the woman seems to be entering into a dream. As she looks into the dark water, a centaur appears whose human and animal parts supposedly symbolize the duality of spirit and body. The centaur then walks about and then throws a spear of light into the center of the stadium, from which a giant statue that exemplifies Cycladic art (and thus one of the first depictions of the human form in Greek art) emerges. This Cycladic head also represents one of the first attempts of humanity to understand itself. With the use of lasers, geometrical shapes and other scientific images (such as a stylistic representation of the Solar System) are displayed on the figure's face. The statue then breaks into pieces that float away, and from within it emerges a smaller kouros statue from the Archaic Period of Greek sculpture, which in turn breaks apart to reveal the depiction of man in a sculpture of the classical period, symbolizing the dawn of individuality and extolling human scale, one of the principal themes of the 2004 Olympics. At the end of this sequence, a cube arises from the water, and a man starts slowly balancing himself on the rotating cube while representations of humankind's greatest achievements, contrasted to humanistic representations and images of people of various ethnicities and ages, are projected onto the pieces of broken sculpture, which seem to be floating above the water. This last sequence is meant to symbolize the birth of logical thought, higher learning, and humanity finally making sense of the world in which it lives. After this sequence, the pieces of sculpture descend to the water, meant to symbolize the Greek isles.

# Former CSU Sprinter Joseph Amoah Selected as Flagbearer for Ghana at 2024 Olympics
### Story Links
**ACCRA, Ghana –** Former Coppin State men's track & field standout **Joseph Amoah** has been selected as the captain and flagbearer for Ghana during the Paris 2024 Olympics, which will take place from July 26 through August 11. Amoah is making his second Olympics appearance at the Games of the XXXIII Olympiad, where he will be competing in the 4x100m Relay.
"I would like to say thank you to the team for selecting me as captain and flagbearer of the opening ceremony," said Amoah. "It's an honor to me. It makes me feel honored and distinguished to have this type of opportunity. I feel like its another milestone in my career. Not a lot of people even get the chance to compete in the Olympics so being able to compete and getting selected as the flagbearer is mindblowing. I can't thank God enough."
Ghana will be presenting nine athletes at this year's Olympics. The heats of the 4x100m will be run on August 8 at 5:35 am ET with the final set for 1:45 pm ET on August 9.
A native of Accra, Ghana, Amoah was a seven-time USTFCCCA All-American and the 2019 and 2021 Mid-Atlantic Region Track Athlete of the Year. At the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, Amoah took 13 th in the 200m with a time of 20.27 in the semifinals. Amoah also anchored the 4x100m Relay to the finals at the Olympics in a national record time of 38.08, chasing down the United States anchor for the final qualifying spot in the final.
Amoah owns personal record times of 9.94 in the 100m dash and 20.08 in the 200m dash while holding Coppin State records in the 100m, 200m, 4x100m, 4x200m and 4x400m Relays.

# Former CSU Sprinter Joseph Amoah Selected as Flagbearer for Ghana at 2024 Olympics
### Story Links
**ACCRA, Ghana –** Former Coppin State men's track & field standout **Joseph Amoah** has been selected as the captain and flagbearer for Ghana during the Paris 2024 Olympics, which will take place from July 26 through August 11. Amoah is making his second Olympics appearance at the Games of the XXXIII Olympiad, where he will be competing in the 4x100m Relay.
"I would like to say thank you to the team for selecting me as captain and flagbearer of the opening ceremony," said Amoah. "It's an honor to me. It makes me feel honored and distinguished to have this type of opportunity. I feel like its another milestone in my career. Not a lot of people even get the chance to compete in the Olympics so being able to compete and getting selected as the flagbearer is mindblowing. I can't thank God enough."
Ghana will be presenting nine athletes at this year's Olympics. The heats of the 4x100m will be run on August 8 at 5:35 am ET with the final set for 1:45 pm ET on August 9.
A native of Accra, Ghana, Amoah was a seven-time USTFCCCA All-American and the 2019 and 2021 Mid-Atlantic Region Track Athlete of the Year. At the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, Amoah took 13 th in the 200m with a time of 20.27 in the semifinals. Amoah also anchored the 4x100m Relay to the finals at the Olympics in a national record time of 38.08, chasing down the United States anchor for the final qualifying spot in the final.
Amoah owns personal record times of 9.94 in the 100m dash and 20.08 in the 200m dash while holding Coppin State records in the 100m, 200m, 4x100m, 4x200m and 4x400m Relays.

Title: Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, who helped end decades of one-party rule in Mexico, dies at 92
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano, a three-time presidential candidate, a central figure in Mexico’s democratic transition and son of former president Lázaro Cárdenas del Río, died in Mexico City on Wednesday. He was 92.
The cause of Cárdenas’ death was not immediately clear. He reportedly passed away in the Ángeles Metropolitano Hospital in the Roma Sur neighborhood of the capital.
President Claudia Sheinbaum and former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador acknowledged Cárdenas’ death in social media posts on Wednesday night.
Sheinbaum called him “a man of steadfast principles who transformed the political life of our country.”
López Obrador said Cárdenas was “a precursor of the democratic movement in Mexico’s recent history.”
“Without him, the country’s political reality would be different,” he wrote.
> La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum encabeza la guardia de honor ante el féretro de Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, histórico líder de la izquierda mexicana, acompañada por la familia del fallecido político.

Cárdenas is credited with helping to end the Institutional Revolutionary Party’s decades-long rule in Mexico, which spanned much of the 20th century. He was a member of the PRI for more than 30 years, but left the party in 1987 and ran in the 1988 presidential election as the candidate for the National Democratic Front, a coalition of left-wing parties. Cárdenas is widely believed to have won that election, but the PRI’s Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner.
He would go on to contest the 1994 and 2000 elections as the candidate for the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), which he co-founded. The 2000 election was won by the National Action Party (PAN) candidate Vicente Fox, who became the first president of Mexico from outside the PRI or its predecessors in 71 years.

## **The early years**
Cárdenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, exactly two months before his father, Lázaro Cárdenas, won the 1934 presidential election with more than 98% of the vote. His mother was Amalia Solórzano Bravo, who, like his father, was a native of Michoacán.
Cárdenas was not yet four years old when his father nationalized Mexico’s oil industry on March 18, 1938. Lázaro Cárdenas is best remembered for that historic decision, but also oversaw significant land reform, redistributing millions of hectares to small-scale farmers, or _campesinos_.
Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas spent his early years living at Los Pinos, the erstwhile residence of the president of Mexico. The New York Times reported that “[a] boyhood friend, José J. Altamirano, remembered the young Cuauhtémoc pushing toy trucks around his father’s feet there.”
Cárdenas was educated at private schools before enrolling in a civil engineering degree at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM). He graduated from UNAM in the mid-1950s and worked as a civil engineer before starting his long political career.
Cárdenas wed María Celeste Batel in 1963 and they remained married until her death in 2021. The couple had three children.

## **A political life**
Cárdenas was a member of the PRI from 1954 to 1987. During that period, he served as a federal senator for Michoacán (1976-80) and governor of Michoacán (1980-86).
While in those positions, he was critical of the federal government’s economic decisions — Mexico’s so-called neoliberal period began in 1982 — and the “_dedazo,”_ the colloquial name for the practice in which the sitting president handpicked the PRI’s next presidential candidate.
Before he left the PRI, Cárdenas, Porfirio Muñoz, Ifigenia Martínez and others founded the Corriente Democrática (Democratic Current), a progressive and reformist faction of the PRI.
Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas at the 100 Hours March in Mexico City in 1987, a protest organized by the Corriente Democrática over the lack of transparency in the selection of PRI presidential candidate Carlos Salinas de Gortari. (Cuartoscuro)

## **The 1988 presidential election**
Cárdenas had hopes of representing the PRI at the 1988 presidential election, but President Miguel de la Madrid chose Salinas de Gortari — a free trade advocate — as the party’s flag bearer.
Having left the PRI, Cárdenas stood as the candidate for the National Democratic Front, which was backed by the Mexican Socialist Party and the Authentic Party of the Mexican Revolution, among other parties and organizations.
His message of economic nationalism resonated with voters, and early results on the night of the 1988 election showed that he had a significant lead over Salinas. However, later in the night, election officials claimed that the electoral computer system had broken down and they stopped reporting results. Before midnight on July 6, 1988, Salinas was declared the winner with almost 51% of the vote compared to Cárdenas’ 31%, according to the official, but highly questionable, results.
De la Madrid admitted that the results were rigged in his 2004 memoir.
The New York Times reported that Cárdenas’ “sway over the Mexican people was so great that he could have, with a few words, set off a bloody civil war after obvious fraud in the 1988 presidential election robbed him of the victory that many believed was his.”
“But instead of whipping up their anger, he convinced his followers that they could launch a true revolution, not by taking to the streets but by returning to the polls.”
> “Se cayó el sistema”.

> La elección presidencial de 1988 marcó para siempre la trayectoria de Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas. La interrupción del flujo de información, las denuncias de fraude y el triunfo oficial de Carlos Salinas de Gortari abrieron una de las mayores polémicas electorales de México.

## **Cárdenas seeks the presidency again**
In 1989, Cárdenas, Porfirio Muñoz, Ifigenia Martínez and Andrés Manuel López Obrador founded the PRD, which became Mexico’s main left-wing party.
Cárdenas represented the PRD at the 1994 and 2000 presidential elections, finishing third in both.
In between his second and third presidential bids, he served as mayor of Mexico City between 1997 and 1999, having won the first direct election of the capital’s head of government, a position previously filled by presidential appointment.
President Sheinbaum used the Mexico City mayorship as a springboard to the presidency, but that wasn’t the case for Cárdenas. Fox took the presidency for the PAN in 2000, which, along with Felipe Calderón’s victory in another controversial election in 2006, left the PRI out of power at the federal level for 12 years. The once-dominant party wouldn’t return to the national halls of power until Enrique Peña Nieto took office in late 2012.
While he didn’t rise to the national leadership position he appeared to be destined for, Cárdenas “was, in a real sense, one of the midwives of Mexico’s democratic transition,” according to University of California political scientist Kathleen Bruhn.
He helped turn the PRD into a competitive political party after the long 20th-century hegemony of the PRI. The party won elections in Mexico City and various states before its recent demise as a result of its poor showing in the 2024 federal elections. Cárdenas left the PRD in 2014, 25 years after co-founding the party, due to differences with its leadership, but he will forever be linked to the party that was Mexico’s preeminent leftist force until the emergence last decade of the National Regeneration Movement, or Morena, which has ruled Mexico since late 2018.
Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas with Andrés Manuel López Obrador at a campaign rally in the Mexico City Zócalo in 2000. (Pedro Mera / Cuartoscuro)

## **Symbol of the Mexican left**
The La Jornada newspaper described Cárdenas as a “symbol of the left in Mexico” and a “historic leader” of the national leftist movement.
“Cárdenas left a profound mark on contemporary political history by leading the most significant rupture of the PRI in the decade of the ’80s, the … Corriente Democrática, and by opening a new stage for the Mexican left,” reported the Mexico City-based daily.
“… He became closely associated with the emergence of an electoral left, the call for free and competitive elections, and the transformation of the Mexican political system. He also supported causes such as those of the EZLN [the Zapatista Army of National Liberation] and the defense of energy resources and national sovereignty,” La Jornada wrote.
El Universal reported that biographers have defined his ideology as “rejection of neoliberalism, defense of the state in strategic sectors, especially energy, austerity, national sovereignty and laicism.”

## **Cárdenas’ autumn years**
Cárdenas remained engaged in Mexican politics in the later years of his life. He spoke out about the need to combat organized crime groups and retake territory they control, and voiced concerns about issues such as low economic growth, the militarization of public security and insufficient funding for education and healthcare.
“I’m very concerned about the situation we’re living, the situation that the country is going through,” he said during a meeting with a cross-party group of senators in 2022. He made those remarks while his former PRD colleague, López Obrador, was in office. Like Cárdenas, AMLO contested three presidential elections, but, in contrast to his political associate, won on his third attempt.
In 2011, Cárdenas, at the age of 77, was awarded the Belisario Domínguez medal, the Mexican Senate’s highest honor, in recognition of his political career and contributions to public life. Among those contributions are several books he authored.
Cárdenas is survived by his three children Cuauhtémoc, Camila and Lázaro Cárdenas Batel, and his grandchildren. Lázaro, governor of Michoacán between 2002 and 2008, is President Sheinbaum’s chief of staff.
_With reports from La Jornada, Reforma, El Economista, El Universal and The New York Times_
